body:
You are drafting spoken lines for a video game. Reply with plain text only, in the exact row format given at the end of this message. Do not send messages to anyone else and do not ask questions: decide. Write nothing but the rows (no title, no notes, no Markdown).

THE GAME. "The Crooked Moon" is a single-player, turn-based tactical party RPG built from a folk-horror Dungeons and Dragons campaign. It is set in Wickermoor Hollow, a haunted valley in Druskenvald, a land of endless night under a giant Crooked Moon with a crone's face. The look is a Halloween that never ends, drawn like an 1980s cartoon. A ghost train, the Ghostlight Express, has crashed in the valley; the party is stranded in the Hollow and its village, Wickermoor. The tone is warm, wry and funny on the surface, with real dread and real grief underneath. The player controls a party of four chosen from six companions: Rook Coldwake, Tobin Hayward, Silas Vane, Delphine Ravelle, Lucan Houndstooth and Cordelia Skein. They are quirky, capable adults.

THE NARRATOR. A NARRATOR row is spoken by the Vagrant, the green-skinned ferryman of the ghost train, who tells the tale in a folksy Southern drawl. At the camp fire he is warm and wry, and when a talk turns sad his humour leaves and he goes plain and level. He speaks to the party as "you" and about the companion in the third person, by first name. Present tense, one or two sentences, under about 32 words. Concrete senses (a smell, a sound, a touch, what the hands are doing) over adjectives. Never tell the player what to feel. Never "suddenly". No facts the party could not see. Drop the final g ("hangin'") in about one Narrator row in four, and use no other dialect spelling. He is kind, never mocks a stumble and never makes light of the dead.

RULES FOR EVERY LINE.
1. The companion's voice sheet below comes first. Match its accent, pace, vocabulary and contractions, and the existing lines. Use a pet phrase at most twice in the whole reply and never twice in one talk. Never repeat or closely paraphrase a line already in the voice sheet or the note.
2. A SAY row is the companion speaking: one or two short sentences, under about 28 words. Never put three sentences in one row; start another row instead.
3. The party's options (OPTION rows) are under 12 words, in the plain voice of the party, work at any hour and in any weather, never name a hero, and are never rolls or checks. A reply must always answer the option it follows.
4. Canon limits. Use only the facts in the voice sheet and the note below. Do not invent a new named person, place, monster, event, object the companion carries, or piece of the companion's history. You may invent small, harmless habits, fondnesses, superstitions and turns of phrase, and the look of the fire and the night. Name no place that the note does not name. Never state a dark secret. You may come close to one and step back.
5. Nothing here is a game system: no dice, no checks, no points, no levels, no HP, no "approval", no menus talked about aloud. Plain punctuation only (commas, full stops, hyphens, apostrophes, question marks, quotation marks inside a line when someone is quoted). No em dashes, no semicolons, no brackets, no asterisks, no stage directions, no placeholders.
6. Humour comes from the character, never explained. The sad turn is plain and short.
7. Our own words. Nothing quoted from any book.

THIS REQUEST. Five camp talks for Lucan, about how Lucan feels about the party and about the road. The talks that depend on how the party treats Lucan are not about any deed in particular. The companion is LUCAN HOUNDSTOOTH (call them Lucan in NARRATOR rows). The attached note is the voice sheet and the fact sheet; it describes an older plan for the Thread's beats in places, so take people, objects, manner and background from it, but where it disagrees with THE FIXED FACTS in this brief, the fixed facts win.

HOW A CAMP TALK WORKS. After a rest the player can walk up to a companion who has asked for a word at the fire. It is private, short and warm. The companion speaks first (NARRATOR and SAY rows), the player chooses what the party says from three short options (or two where the talk says so), and the companion answers in their own voice (a REPLY). Then the talk ends. Nothing in it is a roll or a failure, and every reply must leave the talk finished and the fire going: a cool reply is still an ending, never a slammed door. Each reply also carries a REASON row: one sentence beginning "You", past tense, under 14 words, saying what the party did or said as the companion would remember it (for example "You heard me out at the fire" or "You waved it off and went to bed"). A REASON is plain notice text and is not spoken.

THE TALKS. Write these five talks, in this order, with these keys. Every talk is a private word at the fire in a different mood. Do not repeat a topic across them.

TALK strained. Lucan has lost faith in the party: the party's choices have drifted away from what Lucan holds dear (read the note's "Approval moments" for what they like and dislike). Do not claim a specific deed; speak of "the way things have gone" and name what Lucan cares about. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row (where they sit: apart from the fire, what their hands are doing), then 3 or 4 SAY rows saying what is wrong, in their own voice, stern and hurt, not shouting. Three options: OPTION 1 answers well (listens, owns it, asks them to say what would mend it); OPTION 2 answers coldly; OPTION 3 says nothing (stays by the fire, no words; this reply has NO REASON row and is 1 NARRATOR row plus at most 1 SAY row). Replies: 1 reply row each for the cold one, 2 rows for the good one.

TALK doubt. Lucan is doubtful: not angry, but they have doubts about how the party goes about things. Gentler than strained, more puzzled and wary. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row, then 3 SAY rows. Three options: OPTION 1 answers well (takes the doubt seriously and asks what they would do differently); OPTION 2 answers coldly (a flip remark that brushes the doubt off); OPTION 3 says nothing (stays by the fire, no words; this reply has NO REASON row and is 1 NARRATOR row plus at most 1 SAY row). Replies of 1 or 2 rows for the other two, each with a REASON row.

TALK act1. The first night in Wickermoor, a few hours after the Ghostlight Express crashed. Lucan is still shaken and in their own way trying to be useful. They talk about the crash, the Hollow, the endless night and the Crooked Moon through their own eyes (their trade, their habits, their fears from the note), not about plot. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row, then 6 to 8 SAY rows (a second NARRATOR row is allowed). Three options: OPTION 1 asks how they are holding up; OPTION 2 shares something of the party's own; OPTION 3 says they should get some rest and leaves it there. Replies of 1 to 3 rows, each with a REASON row.

TALK act2. Deep in the troubles of the Hollow: the party has been through a lot and Lucan has seen the party fight, win and lose. Something small has shifted in how Lucan sees these people. Keep to the Hollow in general: name no place and no event except the Crooked House (the haunted manor on the hill, already cleansed) and the crash. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row, then 6 to 8 SAY rows. Three options in the same three roles as act1. Replies of 1 to 3 rows, each with a REASON row.

TALK act3. The last stretch has begun; whatever is coming is close, and everyone knows it. Lucan is weary, truthful and a little funny about it, and says something about what the road has made of them and the party. Name no place and no event except the Hollow in general. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row, then 6 to 8 SAY rows. Three options in the same three roles. Replies of 1 to 3 rows, each with a REASON row.

THE ROW FORMAT (exact). One row per line, rows in this order, nothing else:

TALK <key>
NARRATOR: <line>
SAY: <line>
SAY: <line>
OPTION 1: <what the party says>
OPTION 2: <what the party says>
OPTION 3: <what the party says>
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: <optional line>
SAY: <line>
REASON: You <what the party did>
REPLY 2
...
REPLY 3
...

TALK <key> starts a talk (the keys are given below, exactly). The rows before the first OPTION are the talk's opening. Each REPLY block holds one optional NARRATOR row first, then one or two SAY rows, then a REASON row (and an INSPIRE row where the talk asks for one). Write exactly the talks listed, in the order listed, with the row counts given.

The TALK keys, exactly: strained, doubt, act1, act2, act3.

ATTACHED DOCUMENTS. Two documents come attached to this message; read both before you write. `tasks/crooked-moon-companions/lucan_houndstooth-voice-and-beats.md` holds the voice sheet for LUCAN HOUNDSTOOTH (age, accent, pace, pet phrases, existing lines) and the character file (what Lucan likes and dislikes, the Thread, the dark secret you must never state). `tasks/crooked-moon-companions/lucan_houndstooth-camp-talks.md` holds the camp talks already written for Lucan, as voice examples: do not repeat their topics or lines.
result:
TALK strained
NARRATOR: Lucan sits well back from the firelight, thumbing the brass clasp of his closed field journal while his spectral hound curls tight around his boots.
SAY: I must speak plainly, if you please, though a low growl is pressing rather unpleasantly against my collar.
SAY: The way things have gone on our trail bears no resemblance to the conduct of proper hunters.
SAY: We trample the brush with clattering haste, we bully tethered beasts that cannot flee, and we yield the field when a true predator shows its teeth.
SAY: I cannot walk calmly beside companions who treat the hunt as a brawl in a slaughterhouse.
OPTION 1: You are right. Tell us how to mend our ways.
OPTION 2: We survive however we must. Keep up or stay behind.
OPTION 3: Stay quiet by the fire.
REPLY 1
SAY: Keep your hands gentle toward helpless creatures, read the spoor before you charge, and stand firm when the alpha lunges.
SAY: Do that much, friends, and you shall have my rifle and my manners at your shoulder until the end.
REASON: You owned your missteps and asked how to mend the hunt.
REPLY 2
SAY: Then I shall walk at the rear to guard your flank, though we are no longer hunting as colleagues.
REASON: You brushed off my concerns and told me to keep up.
REPLY 3
NARRATOR: Lucan waits while the birch bark pops in the flames, then tucks his journal deep into his crimson coat.
SAY: Silence is at least quieter in the thicket than our usual approach, if you please.

TALK doubt
NARRATOR: Lucan stands near the edge of the camp, brushin' grey ash from his cuff while his hound watches the dark trees.
SAY: Pardon the interruption, friends, as I am still puzzling over our recent habits in the field.
SAY: We rush past fresh spoor without reading the wind, and we treat every crossroads like a tavern doorway.
SAY: In Edwardia, a hunter who ignores the small noses in the brush does not keep his throat for long.
OPTION 1: Fair warning. How would you have us read the trail?
OPTION 2: Our throats are still whole, so our luck holds.
OPTION 3: Say nothing and watch the embers.
REPLY 1
SAY: Slow your stride at the edge of a clearing, if you please, and listen when a stray beast gives warning.
SAY: Patience is the finest shelter a company can carry under these trees.
REASON: You took my doubts to heart and asked for fieldcraft advice.
REPLY 2
NARRATOR: Lucan clears a low rumble from his throat and adjusts the brim of his tricorn hat.
SAY: Luck is a thin coat in a winter storm, friends, though I pray yours does not tear.
REASON: You laughed off my warning and trusted to luck.
REPLY 3
NARRATOR: Lucan watches the smoke drift toward the pines and rests a gloved palm on his hound's ghostly skull.
SAY: Keep your lanterns trimmed tonight, if you please, whatever path we take tomorrow.

TALK act1
NARRATOR: Lucan kneels beside a pile of twisted iron from the Ghostlight Express, sniffing a splintered sleeper before wiping his fingers on a handkerchief.
SAY: Good heavens, what an extraordinary display of poor railway posture.
SAY: One moment we are taking tea in the carriage, and the next the engine is ploughing the turf of Wickermoor Hollow like a startled boar.
SAY: I have walked the grey lanes of Baskerton in deep winter, yet I have never seen a sky refuse the dawn like this one.
SAY: That Crooked Moon hangs above the village with the sour look of a landlady waiting on overdue rent.
NARRATOR: His spectral hound presses close to his knee, and Lucan steadies his own trembling left hand against his rifle sling.
SAY: Look at the pine needles around Wickermoor, friends, every twig bent toward the dark as if the valley itself were holding its breath.
SAY: Still, the air smells of cold iron and damp moss, which means any quarry on these roads will leave a clean track.
SAY: Hush now, the dark has teeth in this hollow, so we must simply keep our manners sharper than its jaw.
OPTION 1: How are you holding up after that crash?
OPTION 2: None of us expected to wake up in a haunted valley.
OPTION 3: Put the journal away and get some rest tonight.
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: Lucan straightens his lapel with careful fingers, though a brief yellow glint catches the edge of his eyes.
SAY: Quite sound in wind and limb, I assure you, apart from a bruised shoulder and a singing in the ears.
SAY: As long as the lantern oil holds and my hound keeps his nose to the wind, I shall manage splendidly.
REASON: You asked how I was holding up after the wreck.
REPLY 2
SAY: Indeed, friends, it is a rude surprise to step off a train into a nursery tale gone rotten.
SAY: Yet there is great comfort in facing an unfamiliar thicket with capable company at one's elbow.
REASON: You shared your own unease about waking in the Hollow.
REPLY 3
SAY: A sensible prescription, if you please, as a tired eye misreads the brush.
SAY: Take the warm side of the fire, and my hound and I shall keep the first watch.
REASON: You told me to put the ledger away and rest.

TALK act2
NARRATOR: Lucan sits on a dry stump warmin' a tin cup between his gloves while his spectral mastiff stretches out across the moss.
SAY: Ever since we walked out of the Crooked House, I have been revising my early notes on this company.
SAY: When the Ghostlight Express first spilled us into the ditch, I feared we were merely a parcel of lost passengers.
SAY: In Baskerton, I knew seasoned trackers who would have bolted at the first howl from these woods.
SAY: Yet I have watched you take hard blows in the mire, wipe the blood from your sleeves, and step right back into the breach.
SAY: Even when the hollow takes a heavy toll, nobody here abandons a friend to the fog.
SAY: My hound has stopped pacing the perimeter when you sleep, which is the highest compliment a hunting dog can pay.
SAY: Prime specimen of a hunting party, if you please, and I am proud to walk in your stride.
OPTION 1: How are you faring after everything we have faced?
OPTION 2: We only made it this far because we stood together.
OPTION 3: Save your strength for the morning trail.
REPLY 1
SAY: The yellow behind my eyes has been remarkably quiet of late, friends, even when the brush grows loud.
SAY: It is far easier to hold a civilised posture when one is not afraid of standing alone.
REASON: You checked on my spirits deep in the Hollow.
REPLY 2
NARRATOR: Lucan tips his tin cup toward you in a quiet salute, a warm grain in his low voice.
SAY: Quite right, as a pack that holds its line can turn any beast in the forest.
SAY: Whatever waits further down the road will find us hard to scatter.
REASON: You reminded me that we survived by standing together.
REPLY 3
SAY: Most prudent, friends, for the damp air is settling into the boots.
SAY: Sleep deeply, and I shall wake you when the kettle boils.
REASON: You urged me to save my strength for the morning.

TALK act3
NARRATOR: Lucan rests his rifle across his knees with his tricorn off, lettin' the firelight catch the grey at his temples.
SAY: The wind through the Hollow has changed its note tonight, friends, if you care to listen.
SAY: Every bird in the brush has gone still, the way the woods always do before the real quarry steps into the lane.
SAY: When I first buttoned on this crimson coat, I thought a huntsman needed a grand title and a terrible hound to walk the dark.
SAY: Now my coat is mended with plain thread, my boots are scarred to the welt, and I have never felt steadier on my heels.
SAY: This valley strips the swagger off a man until only the bone and the company remain.
SAY: If the yellow takes my eyes in the last thicket, I know you will keep the lantern steady until I find my name again.
SAY: Whatever beast waits at the end of this spoor, it is about to meet very polite ruin.
OPTION 1: How are you holding up before the final push?
OPTION 2: Whatever waits ahead, we finish this hunt side by side.
OPTION 3: Get some sleep while the woods are still quiet.
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: Lucan lets out a soft breath that fogs the cold air, his shoulders easy inside his worn coat.
SAY: Tired in the marrow, if you please, yet my hands have not shaken once since we made camp.
SAY: My hound and I are ready for the whistle whenever you give the word.
REASON: You asked how I was holding up before the end.
REPLY 2
SAY: Side by side it shall be, friends, with clean posture and not a single step yielded.
SAY: Good heavens, I almost pity the creature that tries to part us now.
REASON: You promised we would finish the hunt side by side.
REPLY 3
SAY: I shall turn in presently, once the embers settle to a tidy glow.
SAY: Rest well, friends, and thank you for the road.
REASON: You told me to sleep while the woods were quiet.
